Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction from scarring/fibrosis; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid hypertrophy, **raised amylase**, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → osteoporosis, infertility; cardiac failure, arrhythmic death; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality
Severe starvation → **hypoalbuminemia** with pitting edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

table.title: Diagnostic distinction
rows: Restriction or purging + weight-gain fear/distorted self-image

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.scope: Diagnosis (beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone), unruptured ectopic pregnancy, medical management (methotrexate), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, surgical management
ectopic-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, usually tubal; early pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding requires localization and rupture assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior ectopic, PID/tubal damage, tubal surgery, infertility treatment, smoking
IUDs prevent pregnancy overall; pregnancy despite IUD has higher ectopic proportion; many cases lack risks

rows.label: Clues
items: Amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, spotting; cervical motion/adnexal tenderness nonspecific
★ **Syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritoneal signs, hypotension** → hemoperitoneum/rupture
Heterotopic pregnancy possible despite visualized intrauterine pregnancy, particularly after assisted reproduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired tubal transport → extrauterine trophoblastic implantation, invasion, hemorrhage
Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent DNA synthesis in proliferating trophoblast

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test → quantitative beta-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound**; ultrasound regardless of hCG when symptomatic
Extrauterine yolk sac/embryo diagnostic; adnexal mass/free fluid supportive; empty uterus alone insufficient
★ Stable pregnancy of unknown location → **repeat hCG in 48 hours**, serial ultrasound until resolved/localized
Subnormal 48-hour hCG rise + empty uterus + pain → suspect **ectopic**; rapid fall favors miscarriage
Discriminatory threshold up to 3,500 mIU/mL protects viable IUP; abnormal rise/fall cannot establish location

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/rupture concern → **IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent laparotomy**; do not await serial hCG
Confirmed unruptured, stable, reliable follow-up, hCG <5,000, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal heartbeat → consider **methotrexate**
Avoid methotrexate: viable IUP, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal disease, cytopenias, immunodeficiency, unreliable follow-up
Postmethotrexate hCG days 4/7: fall ≥15% → weekly until negative; inadequate fall → reassess/re-dose/surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, death, tubal loss, recurrence, impaired fertility
Methotrexate: mucositis, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression; rupture remains possible despite falling hCG

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat/prevent STIs, smoking cessation; prior ectopic → early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancy
Methotrexate counseling: avoid alcohol, folate supplements, intercourse until resolution; avoid conception for 3 months
Unsensitized Rh-negative ectopic → Rh(D) immune globulin; provide return precautions for escalating pain/dizziness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Miscarriage: intrauterine pregnancy loss; passage of decidual tissue alone does not prove IUP
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: ovarian source, may coexist with normal pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary

table.title: Alternative definitive branches
rows: Stable, minimal symptoms, low declining hCG
Selected expectant management with reliable surveillance
Heartbeat, high hCG, severe pain, or contraindication

ectopic-pregnancy.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG ectopic pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ectopic-pregnancy), [NICE tubal ectopic management](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG126/chapter/management-of-tubal-ectopic-pregnancy); conservative discriminatory threshold established ACOG teaching.

epididymitis.name: Epididymitis
epididymitis.scope: Acute epididymitis, sexually transmitted vs enteric pathogens by age, Prehn sign, empiric antibiotic regimens, ruling out torsion
epididymitis.core: Gradual unilateral posterior testicular pain with urinary or urethral inflammation suggests epididymitis; always assess for torsion first.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexually active younger adults: gonorrhea/chlamydia; older adults with obstruction/instrumentation: enteric organisms
Insertive anal intercourse permits both STI and enteric pathogens; exposure matters more than age

rows.label: Clues
items: Tender swollen epididymis, dysuria, fever, possible urethral discharge; cremasteric reflex often preserved
Prehn sign: elevation may relieve pain, but **cannot exclude torsion**
Sudden severe onset, nausea, high-riding/horizontal testis → surgical emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ascending urethral/urinary infection spreads through vas deferens → epididymal inflammation
Extension into testis causes epididymo-orchitis; edema can impair perfusion in severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High torsion suspicion → **urgent urology/exploration**, without waiting for testing
Uncertain → **Doppler ultrasound**; epididymal hyperemia favors infection, absent testicular flow favors torsion
★ First-catch urine **gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT**, urinalysis, bacterial urine culture; HIV/syphilis testing
Negative ultrasound does not exclude epididymitis; persistent mass warrants alternative-diagnosis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric antibiotics after specimens; **scrotal support, NSAIDs**, relative rest
Treat before test results; regimen determined by likely pathogens, not age alone
Reevaluate if no improvement within **72 hours**; severe fever/pain or inability to adhere → hospitalization

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess, testicular infarction, chronic scrotal pain, reduced fertility
Persistent swelling after treatment → assess tumor, TB, abscess, infarction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ STI-associated infection: **partners from prior 60 days** need evaluation/presumptive treatment
Abstain until both partners treated and symptoms resolved; condoms reduce reinfection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: abrupt pain, absent reflex; urgent detorsion required
Torsed appendage: focal upper-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign
Inguinal hernia: groin/scrotal mass, bowel symptoms, reducibility or strangulation

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

foreign-body-aspiration.name: Foreign body aspiration
foreign-body-aspiration.scope: Pediatric airway foreign body, choking maneuvers, rigid bronchoscopy, chest x-ray findings (air trapping, atelectasis), observation of partial obstruction
foreign-body-aspiration.core: Abrupt choking with unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests airway foreign body, even with normal radiographs.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Children <3 years exploring objects orally; nuts, seeds, grapes, hot dogs, toy fragments
Neurologic swallowing impairment, sedation, intoxication, poor dentition in adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed coughing/gagging during eating or play; symptoms may partially resolve after initial event
★ **Cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe** → severe airway obstruction
Proximal obstruction: stridor; distal obstruction: focal wheeze, persistent cough, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia
Cyanosis, altered consciousness, exhaustion → imminent respiratory arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Partial ball-valve blockage allows inspiration but limits expiration → distal hyperinflation
Complete bronchial blockage → resorption atelectasis; retained organic material causes inflammation and infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable child → **chest x-ray**, including expiratory or bilateral decubitus views when feasible
Unilateral air trapping, mediastinal shift, collapse, or radiopaque object may identify location
Most food objects are radiolucent; negative examination/imaging does not exclude a convincing history
★ High suspicion → **bronchoscopy**; avoid delaying definitive evaluation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: Effective cough/partial obstruction → encourage coughing, observe closely; no blind finger sweep
★ Infant severe choking: **5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts**, repeat
Age ≥1 year: cycles of five back blows/five abdominal thrusts; pregnancy/marked obesity → chest thrusts
Unresponsive → CPR, inspect mouth during airway opening, remove visible object only
★ Stable retained pediatric object → **rigid bronchoscopy** for retrieval; expert airway team for unstable obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrest, postobstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, granulation tissue
Removal can cause bleeding, edema, or pneumothorax; persistent symptoms need reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid small hard foods/toys; cut grapes lengthwise, supervise eating, avoid running with food
Teach caregivers choking response; keep small objects away from young children

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent diffuse wheeze with bronchodilator response
Croup: preceding URI, barking cough, diffuse upper-airway obstruction
Bronchiolitis: viral prodrome, diffuse crackles/wheezing in an infant

gastric-motility-disorders.name: Gastric motility disorders
gastric-motility-disorders.scope: Gastroparesis (diabetic, idiopathic, postsurgical), gastric emptying study, prokinetic agents (metoclopramide, erythromycin), gastric bezoars, dietary management
gastric-motility-disorders.core: Early satiety, postprandial fullness, and vomiting retained food suggest delayed gastric emptying after mechanical obstruction has been excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Longstanding diabetes with autonomic neuropathy, idiopathic disease, vagal injury after gastric surgery
Opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 receptor agonists; acute hyperglycemia also slows gastric transit

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, bloating, vomiting hours after eating, weight loss; examination may reveal a succussion splash
Erratic nutrient absorption → unpredictable postprandial glucose and hypoglycemia after usual insulin doses
Inability to retain liquids, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities → urgent stabilization
Patchy alopecia from hair pulling + early satiety, vomiting → gastric **trichobezoar**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Disordered antral contraction, pyloric relaxation, and neural signaling impair coordinated meal propulsion
Indigestible material accumulates → gastric bezoar; retained food alone does not establish gastroparesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Upper endoscopy** or imaging first to exclude gastric outlet obstruction
★ Confirm with **4-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy**; >10% retention at 4 hours abnormal
Hold motility-altering drugs and correct marked hyperglycemia before testing; shorter studies can miss disease
Check electrolytes, glucose/A1c, TSH; endoscopy directly identifies obstructing bezoars

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Small, frequent, low-fat, low-fiber meals**; small-particle or liquid nutrition if needed
Correct dehydration/electrolytes, optimize glycemia, stop causative drugs; severe malnutrition → jejunal feeding
★ **Metoclopramide** first-line; extrapyramidal/tardive dyskinesia risk, usually limit to 12 weeks
Short-course erythromycin: tachyphylaxis limits benefit; ondansetron relieves nausea without improving emptying
Bezoar → endoscopic fragmentation/removal; refractory cases → specialist assessment, no routine pyloric botulinum injection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, malnutrition, dehydration, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
Bezoar-related obstruction or ulceration; erythromycin → QT prolongation and drug interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid high-fiber indigestible foods and excessive fat; dietitian support and weight monitoring
Coordinate mealtime insulin with actual food absorption; avoid unnecessary long-term opioids

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastric outlet obstruction: focal transition, intrinsic stenosis, or extrinsic mass rather than isolated transit delay
Rumination: effortless regurgitation soon after meals without preceding nausea
Functional dyspepsia: similar fullness with normal emptying and no structural cause

gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
gastroenteritis.scope: Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus), foodborne illness, bacterial enteritis, traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), oral rehydration therapy, dehydration assessment
gastroenteritis.core: Acute vomiting and diarrhea usually need hydration and selective testing; shock, blood, focal pain, or systemic toxicity changes the approach.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, childcare or institutional outbreaks
Infants, older adults and immunocompromised people have greater dehydration or invasive-infection risk
Pet reptiles → nontyphoidal Salmonella; young infants prone to bacteremia

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools and diffuse cramps favor noninvasive disease; fever or dysentery suggests inflammatory enteritis
Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine; children → fewer wet diapers, absent tears
★ Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension → **severe dehydration/shock**
Toddler + high fever, bloody diarrhea, **seizure** → Shigella; HUS appears days later with hemolysis/AKI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal secretion or epithelial injury causes water/electrolyte losses
Sodium–glucose cotransport remains functional, allowing oral rehydration despite ongoing diarrhea

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild self-limited illness → **no routine stool tests**
Stool PCR/culture and Shiga toxin for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe pain or sepsis
Electrolytes/creatinine for severe dehydration; C difficile testing after antibiotics or healthcare exposure
Persistent >14 days or relevant travel → evaluate parasites; focal/peritoneal pain → imaging for surgical cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral rehydration solution**, frequent small volumes; continue breastfeeding and usual diet
Shock/severe dehydration or failed oral intake → IV isotonic crystalloid; reassess perfusion
Ondansetron can enable oral hydration; avoid juice/soda as primary replacement
Moderate/severe travelers’ diarrhea → azithromycin; suspected STEC → no antibiotics
Loperamide only selected adults with afebrile nonbloody diarrhea; avoid children and inflammatory disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities; postinfectious lactose intolerance
STEC → HUS with hemolysis, low platelets and AKI; invasive bacteria → bacteremia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap/water, food safety, **rotavirus vaccination** in infancy
Norovirus outbreaks: environmental disinfection; food handlers remain off work ≥48 hours after symptoms resolve

rows.label: Mimics
items: Appendicitis/intussusception: localized or episodic severe pain disproportionate to diarrhea
DKA: hyperglycemia, ketones; IBD: persistent bloody diarrhea and weight loss

table.title: Common noninvasive enteritis
rows: Vomiting followed by substantial watery diarrhea

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder
Hysterectomy/pelvic surgery → ureteral ligation: flank pain, fever, unilateral hydroureteronephrosis; not pyelonephritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention, perineal/scrotal hematoma or high-riding prostate → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Blunt flank trauma → **urinalysis**; stable, no hematuria → **no further testing** unless high-energy deceleration
Stable gross hematuria, or microscopic + hypotension → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images, not laparotomy
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; absent flow or high clinical suspicion → immediate exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

gonococcal-infection.name: Gonococcal infection
gonococcal-infection.scope: Urethritis/cervicitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, gonococcal arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis
gonococcal-infection.core: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes mucosal infection and can disseminate into a dermatitis-tenosynovitis-arthritis syndrome or purulent septic arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: New/multiple partners, inconsistent barriers, prior STI, younger age
Complement deficiency increases dissemination risk; neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; rectal/pharyngeal disease often asymptomatic
★ **Migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules** → disseminated infection
Neonate: copious purulent conjunctivitis 2–5 days after birth; corneal injury can progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci adhere to mucosa; antigenic variation permits recurrent infection
Ascending genital spread or bacteremia extends disease beyond initial exposure site

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT at exposed sites**: urine/vaginal, rectal, pharyngeal; test chlamydia, HIV, syphilis
Symptomatic male urethral Gram stain may show intracellular diplococci; less reliable at other sites
Dissemination: blood/synovial cultures and mucosal NAAT; negative joint culture does not exclude diagnosis
Suspected treatment failure → culture and antimicrobial susceptibility, assess reinfection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once**; ≥150 kg → 1 g once
Chlamydia not excluded → doxycycline 7 days, don't await results; pregnancy, older exam questions → azithromycin
★ Disseminated disease → **IV/IM ceftriaxone**, hospitalization initially; drain purulent joint
Neonatal infection → systemic ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime if bilirubin/calcium concerns; topical treatment alone insufficient

rows.label: Complications
items: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, epididymitis, corneal perforation
Rare endocarditis/meningitis; untreated septic arthritis damages cartilage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; abstain 7 days after treatment and until partners treated
Retest at 3 months; pharyngeal test-of-cure at 7–14 days; routine urogenital test-of-cure unnecessary
Condoms, risk-based screening; neonatal erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chlamydia: similar urethritis/cervicitis, NAAT distinguishes
Reactive arthritis: sterile arthritis after infection, conjunctivitis/enthesitis
Staphylococcal arthritis: usually isolated hot joint without migratory skin-tendon syndrome

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute crystal flare → **indomethacin/other NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; joint steroid after excluding infection
NSAID failure → switch class; older exam questions may expect potent NSAID, e.g. indomethacin
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Urate lowering doesn't treat flares; continue through flares; may start mid-flare (older exam questions: wait)

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring; not for isolated hyperuricemia
Uncomplicated first flare → **limit alcohol/fructose**, lose weight; thiazide → losartan; keep indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

head-and-neck-cancer.name: Head and neck cancer
head-and-neck-cancer.scope: Oral cavity cancer, laryngeal cancer, pharyngeal cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, tobacco and alcohol risk, HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma
head-and-neck-cancer.core: Persistent hoarseness, unilateral throat/ear symptoms, a nonhealing oral lesion, or an adult neck mass requires malignancy evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco, alcohol: each independent, dose-dependent squamous cancer risk, synergistic together; betel nut in some populations
HPV exposure drives many oropharyngeal cancers; EBV associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcer or red/white plaque persisting >2–3 weeks; dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss
★ **Adult persistent lateral neck mass** may be metastatic carcinoma, even when cystic
Unilateral referred otalgia with normal otoscopy; hemoptysis or stridor indicates advanced local disease
Nasopharyngeal disease → unilateral serous otitis, epistaxis or cranial neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal squamous transformation and lymphatic spread; field carcinogenesis produces synchronous/second primary tumors

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Direct visualization and biopsy** of mucosal lesion; flexible nasolaryngoscopy for inaccessible sites
Neck mass → contrast CT/MRI plus **fine-needle aspiration**; avoid initial open biopsy
Oropharyngeal tumor → p16/HPV testing; staging imaging assesses regional nodes and distant metastases
Persistent hoarseness → laryngoscopy; no prolonged empiric reflux treatment when malignancy clues present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway compromise/stridor → **secure airway** with ENT/anesthesia support
Early localized cancer → surgery or radiation according to site and function
Locally advanced → combined surgery/radiation with cisplatin-based systemic treatment or definitive chemoradiation
Nasopharyngeal cancer → chemoradiation; recurrent/metastatic disease → systemic treatment, often checkpoint inhibitor

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, airway obstruction, malnutrition, carotid bleeding; nodal/distant metastases
Radiation → xerostomia, dental decay, osteoradionecrosis; surgery → speech/swallow impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Smoking/alcohol cessation, HPV vaccination; dental assessment before head/neck radiation
Swallowing rehabilitation, nutrition support; surveillance for recurrence and second primary cancer

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laryngitis: brief postviral hoarseness resolving with recovery
Branchial cleft cyst: benign developmental lesion; new adult cystic mass still needs cancer exclusion

head-and-neck-cancer.evidence: Neck-mass evaluation checked 2026-10-30: [AAO-HNS adult neck-mass guideline](https://www.entnet.org/quality-practice/quality-products/clinical-practice-guidelines/evaluation-of-the-neck-mass-in-adults/); oncology: established teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles or wheeze (cardiac asthma), dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Low effective volume → baroreceptor-driven nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease
Alveolar flooding → V/Q mismatch, widened A-a gradient, hypoxemia
High-output HF: severe anemia, AV fistula (larger fistula → more shunt); HF signs with **normal/high EF**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Congested HFrEF → loop diuretic + **ACE inhibitor/ARNI first**; beta-blocker/MRA once compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI: 36-hour washout
MRA: eGFR >30, K <5; never ACE inhibitor + ARB; EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD
HFrEF foundation drugs lower mortality; loop diuretics, nitrates alone, digoxin relieve symptoms only

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain
ARDS: diffuse infiltrates, no cephalization; massive crystalloid + **cephalization/perihilar fullness** → volume overload

table.title: Chronic phenotypes
rows: Sacubitril/valsartan (or ACEi/ARB), carvedilol/metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, dapagliflozin

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus
Large hematoma/cephalhematoma resorption → bilirubin overproduction, indirect jaundice

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect, even Coombs-positive → **phototherapy** first; exchange: failure, critical level, encephalopathy
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin; newborn ABO: mother O, baby A/B, Coombs-positive
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound
Physiologic jaundice: indirect, after 24 h, peaks days 3–5, thriving; transient UGT immaturity
Breast-milk jaundice: indirect, thriving; direct elevation excludes it

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation
High filtered calcium exceeds tubular reabsorption → **hypercalciuria** → calcium stones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **Denosumab** (favored, esp renal limitation/refractory) or **IV zoledronic acid/pamidronate** for sustained malignancy control
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul (deep) breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema (Cushing triad), hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine, labetalol, or nitroprusside**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.name: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.scope: Chronic and gestational HTN, preeclampsia, HELLP, eclampsia
hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy-associated hypertension; maternal organ injury or placental dysfunction signals danger even without substantial proteinuria.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, CKD, diabetes, SLE/APS, multifetal gestation
Nulliparity, obesity, age ≥35, family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, visual disturbance, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea; edema nonspecific
★ Severe features: **platelets <100,000/µL**, creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubled, transaminases ≥2× normal
Other severe features: pulmonary edema, refractory neurologic symptoms
Presentation through **6 weeks postpartum**; eclampsia/HELLP possible without prior HTN

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal spiral-artery remodeling → placental ischemia → systemic endothelial injury, vasospasm, capillary leak

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **BP ≥140/90**, either component, twice ≥4 h apart; severe ≥160/110 confirmed within minutes
CBC/platelets, creatinine, AST/ALT, urine protein; fetal growth US + antenatal testing
Proteinuria: **≥300 mg/24 h** or protein/creatinine ≥0.3; dipstick 2+ only if quantification unavailable
Chronic HTN + new proteinuria/end-organ injury → superimposed preeclampsia; HELLP: smear, LDH ≥600 IU/L

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Persistent severe BP ≥15 min → **IV labetalol/hydralazine** or immediate-release oral nifedipine within 30–60 min
★ Severe preeclampsia/eclampsia → **magnesium sulfate** through 24 h postpartum; airway before delivery
Chronic HTN ≥140/90 → oral labetalol/extended-release nifedipine; avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Mg toxicity: areflexia/hypoventilation → stop infusion, **IV calcium gluconate**; oliguria → reduce dose

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, abruption, DIC, AKI, hepatic hematoma/rupture; fetal growth restriction, prematurity, death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High risk or multiple moderate risks → **aspirin 81 mg/day**, start 12–28 wk, ideally before 16
Postpartum BP review within 72 h if severe, otherwise 7–10 days; long-term cardiovascular follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: TTP: profound thrombocytopenia/hemolysis, persists after delivery
Acute fatty liver: hypoglycemia, jaundice, marked coagulopathy
Epilepsy: established seizure disorder; evaluate alternative causes despite obstetric context

table.title: Classification and delivery
rows: Before 20 wk or persists >12 wk postpartum
After 20 wk + proteinuria OR severe features
Severe BP alone sufficient; <34 stable → betamethasone
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets
Deliver after stabilization, any gestational age

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, family history of autoimmune disease; thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass
Congenital primary → **thyroid dysgenesis** most common, not lymphocytic thyroiditis

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease
Infant: macroglossia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle → **TSH/free T4**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic infiltration; firm painless goiter, even if euthyroid; **anti-TPO/antithyroglobulin** antibodies

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Fasting, apart from calcium/iron; TSH at 6–8 weeks; **persistently high → increase dose**, even if asymptomatic
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical, untreated: generally start at TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression, dementia, psychosis: normal TSH; hypothyroidism itself can cause reversible cognitive or psychiatric symptoms
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

impaired-physician.name: Impaired physician
impaired-physician.scope: Acute impairment, substance use, patient safety protection, physician health programs, mandatory reporting to state medical board
impaired-physician.core: Patient safety first when a colleague's ability to practice safely is compromised.

rows.label: Principle
items: Impairment = functional inability to practice safely from illness, substances, or cognitive decline

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Acute intoxication → stop patient contact, arrange coverage, notify supervisor immediately
★ Document objective observations and affected encounters through institutional channels
★ **Physician health program** → evaluation, treatment, monitoring, and safe return to practice

rows.label: Don't
items: Conceal unsafe care or delay intervention while seeking definitive proof
Permit impaired colleague to drive home

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Report to **state medical board** when law requires or ongoing danger remains unaddressed
PHP confidentiality and reporting exemptions vary by jurisdiction

rows.label: Traps
items: Substance use history or treatment alone ≠ current impairment
Employee assistance referral alone insufficient during an immediate patient safety threat

impaired-physician.evidence: Checked AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 9.3.2.

infective-endocarditis.name: Infective endocarditis
infective-endocarditis.scope: Native and prosthetic valve endocarditis, Duke criteria, prophylaxis, IV drug use endocarditis, blood culture diagnostic criteria
infective-endocarditis.core: Persistent bacteremia with valve infection causes systemic emboli, valve destruction, and immune-complex injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, congenital valve abnormality, intracardiac device
Injection drug use → tricuspid involvement; healthcare exposure, indwelling vascular access

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, new regurgitant murmur, embolic stroke, splenic infarct, hematuria
Janeway lesions painless; Osler nodes painful; Roth spots retinal; splinter hemorrhages nonspecific
★ **New conduction block** → periannular abscess; right-sided disease → septic pulmonary emboli

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Endothelial injury → platelet-fibrin nidus → microbial adherence and vegetation
Immune complexes → glomerulonephritis; infected fragments disseminate through downstream circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Three blood-culture sets before antibiotics**; separate peripheral draws unless resuscitation would be delayed
Major microbiology: **typical organism in ≥2 culture sets**, nontypical in ≥3; specialized serology/PCR also qualifies
★ **TTE → TEE** if prosthesis/high suspicion; major imaging: vegetation, abscess, perforation, new significant regurgitation
Definite clinical Duke: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria
Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena, nondiagnostic microbiology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for acutely ill/healthcare-associated cases; tailor to cultures and setting
MSSA → nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin; susceptible viridans streptococci → ceftriaxone
Prolonged pathogen-directed IV antibiotics; prosthetic infections need specialist regimen and early surgical evaluation
Surgery: heart failure, abscess, persistent bacteremia, fungal infection, or selected recurrent/large embolizing vegetations

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute regurgitation, heart failure, mycotic aneurysm, metastatic infection
Antibiotic nephrotoxicity, line infection; hemorrhage into embolic cerebral lesions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dental **amoxicillin** for prosthetic valve/material, previous IE, selected cyanotic/residual CHD, transplant valvulopathy
Good oral hygiene, sterile access; no routine prophylaxis for GI/GU procedures or isolated MVP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: cancer/autoimmune disease, sterile cultures
Atrial myxoma: positional obstruction, intracavitary mass; vasculitis: no infected vegetation

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

inguinal-hernia.name: Inguinal hernia
inguinal-hernia.scope: Direct inguinal hernia, indirect inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, incarcerated and strangulated hernia, physical exam, elective vs emergent surgical repair
inguinal-hernia.core: A groin bulge enlarging with strain suggests hernia; a painful irreducible mass with obstructive or ischemic signs requires urgent surgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Male sex, family history, prematurity, persistent processus vaginalis
Age-related fascial weakness, chronic cough, constipation, heavy strain; femoral hernias more frequent in women

rows.label: Clues
items: Bulge or dragging discomfort with standing/Valsalva, improving supine or after reduction
Incarcerated: contents cannot be reduced; bowel obstruction causes vomiting, distention, obstipation
★ **Severe persistent pain**, tenderness, erythema, toxicity/peritonitis → impaired perfusion; fever may be late

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abdominal contents protrude through a weak opening; a narrow neck impairs venous then arterial perfusion
Richter hernia traps only bowel-wall segment; ischemia may occur without complete obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Standing groin examination with cough/Valsalva**; inspect both sides and assess reducibility
Uncertain occult lesion → dynamic ultrasound; CT if obstruction, complication, or alternative diagnosis suspected
Clinical strangulation → immediate operation; imaging must not delay treatment
Do not rely on surface examination alone to reliably distinguish direct from indirect anatomy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Strangulation → **IV fluids, NPO, analgesia, antibiotics, emergency repair**; resect nonviable bowel
Incarceration without ischemic features → urgent surgeon evaluation; gentle reduction only in selected cases
★ Symptomatic inguinal hernia → **elective mesh repair** in adults; children → herniotomy
Minimally symptomatic men may choose watchful waiting with return precautions
Women and femoral hernias → timely repair because occult femoral disease and strangulation risk are greater

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel obstruction, ischemic necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Repair → chronic groin pain, recurrence, wound/mesh infection, testicular ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and chronic cough, smoking cessation, weight management; risk reduction cannot close an existing defect
After reduction or observation: urgent return for escalating pain, vomiting, or loss of reducibility

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphadenopathy: discrete solid nodes without cough impulse
Hydrocele: transilluminates; confined fluid rather than reducible bowel
Saphena varix: compressible venous swelling; Doppler demonstrates venous flow

table.title: Anatomic distinctions
rows: Below inguinal ligament, medial femoral vein

innocent-murmurs.name: Innocent murmurs
innocent-murmurs.scope: Still murmur, venous hum, physiologic peripheral pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary flow murmur, benign vs pathologic features, reassurance
innocent-murmurs.core: Incidental flow sound in an otherwise healthy child; distinguish normal hemodynamics from structural heart disease using examination and positional maneuvers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childhood; fever, anemia, exercise, anxiety → increased flow and audibility
Prematurity favors physiologic branch pulmonary artery narrowing

rows.label: Clues
items: Soft, localized, short systolic sound; normal pulses, growth, oxygenation, S2; no thrill
★ **Diastolic, holosystolic, harsh, or ≥grade 3** → evaluate for pathology
★ Exertional syncope, chest pain, cyanosis, poor feeding, or growth failure → **cardiology referral**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Normal blood-flow vibrations without valve dysfunction, shunting, or chamber pressure overload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Auscultation supine and standing**; assess femoral pulses, BP, family sudden-death history
Classic benign examination in older child → clinical diagnosis; routine ECG/CXR add little
Uncertain findings or persistent neonatal murmur → pediatric cardiology; **echocardiography** defines structural lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance**; unrestricted sports and usual childhood activities
No cardiac drugs, endocarditis prophylaxis, or serial imaging after confident benign diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: No heart failure or progression to structural disease; mistaken labeling → anxiety and unnecessary activity restriction

rows.label: Mimics
items: ASD: fixed split S2; pulmonary stenosis: ejection click
PDA: unvarying machinery sound; bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: louder with standing or Valsalva; concerning family history

table.title: Benign patterns
rows: Disappears supine or with jugular compression

interstitial-lung-disease.name: Interstitial lung disease
interstitial-lung-disease.scope: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconioses, restrictive PFTs (reduced DLCO, normal/high FEV1/FVC), high-resolution CT
interstitial-lung-disease.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and inspiratory crackles suggest diffuse parenchymal lung disease; HRCT patterns and exposure history identify the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age >60 and smoking: IPF; autoimmune disease; familial fibrosis
Amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin; occupational silica/coal/asbestos, organic antigens; prior thoracic radiation

rows.label: Clues
items: Fine basal Velcro crackles, exertional desaturation, later clubbing; systemic rheumatic features can reveal cause
Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar adenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum, sometimes hypercalcemia
Rapidly worsening oxygenation → infection, embolism, edema, or acute exacerbation evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar/interstitial injury and aberrant repair reduce lung compliance and gas-transfer capacity
Granulomatous inflammation or fibrogenic dust responses produce distinct imaging distributions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **HRCT + full PFTs** after chest radiograph; obtain detailed drug, occupation, hobby, autoimmune history
★ **↓TLC, ↓DLCO, normal/↑FEV1/FVC** support restriction; low FVC alone is insufficient
UIP: basal subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing; exclude known causes before labeling IPF
Autoantibodies when connective-tissue disease suspected; BAL/biopsy selected through multidisciplinary review
Typical UIP without secondary cause may avoid surgical biopsy; assess exertional oxygen needs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Remove offending exposure/drug**, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen for hypoxemia; treat identified cause
★ IPF: **nintedanib or pirfenidone** slows decline; no routine chronic prednisone-based immunosuppression
Inflammatory sarcoid/autoimmune disease: selected steroids or steroid-sparing agents; mild sarcoid may need observation
Progressive fibrotic non-IPF disease → nintedanib consideration; advanced disease → early transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, exacerbations; asbestos raises lung cancer/mesothelioma risk
Silicosis increases TB susceptibility; antifibrotics can cause GI adverse effects and liver injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory immunizations, occupational dust controls, medication monitoring; follow FVC/DLCO trends

rows.label: Mimics
items: Heart failure: congestion/cardiomegaly, volume response; emphysema: obstruction with hyperinflation
Neuromuscular restriction: low volumes with relatively preserved diffusion capacity

table.title: Imaging clues to etiology
rows: Centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, air trapping

invasive-fungal-infections.name: Invasive fungal infections
invasive-fungal-infections.scope: Invasive aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), mucormycosis, candidemia, amphotericin B, voriconazole, systemic corticosteroids
invasive-fungal-infections.core: Fungal syndromes range from allergic airway disease to lethal tissue invasion; immune status and imaging guide testing and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prolonged neutropenia/transplant → molds; DKA, glucocorticoids or iron overload → mucormycosis
Central lines, TPN, abdominal surgery, broad antibiotics → invasive Candida
ABPA: asthma or cystic fibrosis; hypersensitivity rather than tissue invasion
Old TB cavity → **aspergilloma**: mobile fungus ball, air crescent, hemoptysis; colonization, not invasion

rows.label: Clues
items: Invasive aspergillosis: fever despite antibiotics, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, pulmonary nodules
★ **Black nasal/palatal eschar**, facial pain, ophthalmoplegia → rhinocerebral mucormycosis
Candidemia: sepsis, persistent positive blood cultures; metastatic eye, heart or deep-organ infection
ABPA: recurrent wheeze, brown mucus plugs, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Angioinvasive molds cause vascular thrombosis, infarction and necrosis
Candida translocates through damaged gut or colonizes intravascular devices, then disseminates hematogenously
