Cancer pain: escalating requests → tolerance/progression, not addiction; past OUD never limits analgesia

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

table.title: Care settings
rows: Adjust with hospice team; avoid readmission

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may show **double-duct** (bile + pancreatic) dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen
Massive watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, flushing

pancreatic-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established pancreatic oncology teaching.

panic-disorder.name: Panic disorder
panic-disorder.scope: Panic attack criteria, unexpected recurrent attacks, agoraphobia, acute abortive therapy, maintenance therapy, medical rule-outs
panic-disorder.core: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of fear of recurrence or maladaptive behavioral change establish panic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, family history, trauma, anxiety sensitivity
Caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, withdrawal can provoke paniclike symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt intense fear peaks within minutes; palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, derealization
Attack requires ≥4 characteristic symptoms; fear of dying/losing control common
★ **Syncope, exertional onset, hypoxemia, focal findings**, sustained arrhythmia → medical cause until evaluated
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 situations where escape/help seems difficult, persisting ≥6 months

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Threat-circuit overactivation and catastrophic interpretation of benign sensations amplify autonomic symptoms
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ → lightheadedness, perioral/distal tingling; avoidance reinforces anticipatory fear
**Sodium lactate infusion** provokes attacks: heightened panic sensitivity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after medical/substance review**; unexpected episodes distinguish disorder from predictable triggers
Vital signs, examination, ECG for cardiopulmonary symptoms; glucose/TSH or toxicology guided by history
Chest pain risk → ACS/PE evaluation rather than automatic psychiatric attribution
Assess depression, suicidality, substance use; agoraphobia may be diagnosed separately

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ During attack → **calm reassurance, slow breathing**, reduce stimulation after excluding danger
Severe acute episode → short-term lorazepam when needed; avoid with sedatives or substance-use risk
★ Maintenance → **CBT with interoceptive exposure and/or SSRI**, such as sertraline
Start SSRI low, titrate slowly; benefit takes weeks; venlafaxine alternative
Continue effective treatment after remission, then gradual taper; benzodiazepines not preferred long-term

rows.label: Complications
items: Agoraphobic avoidance, impaired function, depression, self-medication with alcohol
Benzodiazepine dependence/withdrawal; alprazolam → **between-dose rebound anxiety**; SSRIs may initially increase anxiety

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**, regular sleep/exercise, practice exposure and relapse-prevention skills
Paper-bag rebreathing discouraged (hypoxemia risk); older exam questions may expect it if SpO₂ normal

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent tremor, heat intolerance, low TSH
SVT: documented abrupt regular tachycardia, not solely subjective palpitations
Social anxiety: fear tied to scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks
Mitral valve prolapse: incidental click/murmur; doesn't explain recurrent attacks with fear of recurrence

panic-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR and anxiety treatment teaching.

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

parenteral-nutrition.name: Parenteral nutrition
parenteral-nutrition.scope: Enteral vs parenteral nutrition indications, parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis, biliary sludge, refeeding syndrome, trace mineral deficiencies
parenteral-nutrition.core: Intravenous nutrition when the gastrointestinal tract cannot safely provide sufficient calories and nutrients.

rows.label: Interpret
items: Prolonged PN plus absent enteral stimulation → cholestasis and gallbladder sludge
Direct bilirubin elevation → evaluate sepsis and obstruction; optimize PN and advance enteral feeds
Monitor glucose, electrolytes, triglycerides, liver tests and catheter complications

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Functional accessible gut → **enteral feeding** to preserve gut function and lower infectious risk
Obstruction, prolonged ileus, short bowel, inaccessible gut or high-output fistula → consider PN
Full or prolonged PN generally requires central access; peripheral PN limited by osmolarity

rows.label: Compare
items: Zinc depletion: dermatitis, poor wound healing; excess GI losses increase requirements
Copper depletion: anemia and neutropenia; selenium depletion: cardiomyopathy
Include vitamins and trace elements; individualize supplementation and monitor long-term levels

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Refeeding after starvation: insulin shifts **phosphate**, potassium and magnesium intracellularly
★ High risk → thiamine before dextrose, replace electrolytes, start calories low and advance slowly
Refeeding also occurs with enteral feeding; severe depletion can cause respiratory failure or arrhythmia

parenteral-nutrition.evidence: Checked ASPEN consensus recommendations for refeeding syndrome (2020).

pediatric-abdominal-masses.name: Pediatric abdominal masses
pediatric-abdominal-masses.scope: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma, WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann), neuroblastoma (adrenal medulla, crosses midline, catecholamines, N-myc), hydronephrosis, hepatoblastoma, ultrasound evaluation
pediatric-abdominal-masses.core: A child's abdominal mass: establish its organ of origin before biopsy; renal, sympathetic, hepatic, and obstructive lesions require different management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Wilms: **WAGR**—aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability
Wilms: Beckwith-Wiedemann—macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia
Hepatoblastoma: very low birth weight, Beckwith-Wiedemann, familial adenomatous polyposis
Hydronephrosis: congenital urinary obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux

rows.label: Clues
items: Often found incidentally during bathing; persistent enlargement, weight loss, pallor suggest malignancy
Neuroblastoma dissemination: periorbital ecchymoses, bone pain; opsoclonus-myoclonus possible
★ Weakness, gait change, bladder dysfunction → possible spinal cord compression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Wilms: embryonal renal tumor; neuroblastoma: neural crest-derived adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain
Hepatoblastoma: embryonal hepatic malignancy; hydronephrosis: collecting-system dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** first → solid versus cystic and renal versus extrarenal origin
Solid lesion → contrast CT/MRI abdomen; chest imaging for malignant staging
Neuroblastoma: tissue diagnosis, MYCN testing, MIBG imaging, bone marrow assessment for staging
MYCN amplification → unfavorable prognosis; age and stage also determine neuroblastoma risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wilms: avoid repeated vigorous palpation and routine percutaneous biopsy; US approach usually nephrectomy first
Wilms: surgery + vincristine/dactinomycin-based chemotherapy; radiation for higher-risk disease
Neuroblastoma: low risk → observation/resection; high risk → chemotherapy, surgery, transplant, anti-GD2 immunotherapy
Hepatoblastoma: cisplatin-based chemotherapy + resection; unresectable liver-confined disease → transplant evaluation
Hydronephrosis: infected obstruction → urgent drainage; progressive functional loss → corrective surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Tumor rupture/spillage worsens Wilms staging; bilateral disease threatens renal function
Hydronephrosis → infection, renal injury; neuroblastoma → marrow failure or cord compression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Syndrome-specific abdominal ultrasound surveillance for children predisposed to embryonal tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Constipation: fecal loading, improves after stool evacuation
Ovarian mass: pelvic/adnexal origin; torsion causes acute pain

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

perioperative-care.name: Perioperative care
perioperative-care.scope: Preoperative cardiac risk, pulmonary evaluation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, medication management, pain control
perioperative-care.core: Optimize active disease, estimate procedural and patient risk, and order testing only when the result could change perioperative management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **MI within 60 days**, decompensated HF → highest perioperative cardiac risk; older exam questions may expect MI within 6 months
Emergency, vascular or intrathoracic surgery; ischemic heart disease, heart failure, CKD, diabetes
Smoking, COPD, OSA, frailty, malnutrition and prior anesthesia complications

rows.label: Clues
items: Chest pain, new dyspnea, syncope or decompensated fluid overload require targeted evaluation
Poor functional capacity: inability to climb stairs or perform activities around 4 METs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Surgical stress raises myocardial oxygen demand; anesthesia can lower perfusion pressure
Sedation, pain and recumbency reduce ventilation and promote atelectasis and venous stasis
Surgical stress, pain, opioids → nonosmotic **ADH** release → transient oliguria with normal renal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RCRI/NSQIP** plus functional assessment; no routine stress test for low-risk surgery
Elevated risk, poor/unknown capacity → stress test if management changes; cannot exercise → **pharmacologic stress imaging**
ECG for cardiovascular symptoms; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease
No routine chest radiograph/spirometry without respiratory findings; assess airway and OSA history
Lung resection: **predicted postoperative FEV1** best predictor of complications; predicted postoperative FEV1 <30–40% → high risk, exercise testing before deciding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Active ACS, decompensated HF or unstable arrhythmia → defer elective surgery and stabilize
★ Continue chronic **beta blockers/statins**; do not start beta blockade on surgery day
Hold **SGLT2 inhibitors 3–4 days**; individualize GLP-1 drugs by aspiration risk; continue reduced basal insulin
★ **Cefazolin within 60 minutes** before incision; MRSA or severe beta-lactam allergy → vancomycin within 120 minutes
Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen, regional block, selective NSAID; add opioid by severity, respiratory monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial injury, AKI, delirium, pneumonia, VTE and surgical-site infection
Opioids aggravate OSA; excessive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema
New postoperative dyspnea, ↓basal breath sounds → chest radiograph first, before PE imaging or heparin

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lung expansion exercises, early mobilization, mechanical/pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis
Anticoagulation interruption individualized; bridging reserved for highest thrombotic risk
Chronic steroid exposure with adrenal suppression → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage
Usable gut → **enteral feeding**, including distal jejunostomy, over TPN

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anxiety-related dyspnea: normal cardiopulmonary evaluation
Stable chronic disease: baseline symptoms alone do not mandate cancellation

table.title: Postoperative pain
rows: Severe pain after major abdominal surgery

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

personality-disorders.name: Personality disorders
personality-disorders.scope: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), Cluster B (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic), Cluster C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD), dialectical behavior therapy
personality-disorders.core: Enduring, inflexible patterns of cognition, affect, relationships, or impulse control cause impairment across settings beginning by adolescence or early adulthood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperament, genetic susceptibility, early adversity and disrupted attachment; avoid attributing diagnosis to trauma alone
Traits must exceed cultural expectations; diagnose cautiously during acute illness or developmental transitions

rows.label: Clues
items: Cluster A: paranoid—distrust; schizoid—detachment; schizotypal—magical thinking, odd speech/perceptions, social discomfort
Cluster B: antisocial—violations of rights; histrionic—attention seeking; narcissistic—grandiosity/entitlement
Cluster C: avoidant—fears rejection/embarrassment, avoids new activities; dependent—clinging; OCPD—rigid perfectionism, control
★ Borderline: **splitting, unstable identity/relationships, self-harm**, abandonment fear, chronic emptiness, impulsivity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maladaptive trait patterns impair emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning; no diagnostic biomarker
Impulsive aggression, violent suicide → **low CSF 5-HIAA** (serotonin metabolite)

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Longitudinal clinical assessment** across contexts; obtain collateral with consent
Exclude mood episodes, psychotic illness, substances, neurodevelopmental disorders and acquired brain disease
★ Antisocial diagnosis requires **age ≥18 plus conduct disorder before 15**
Borderline may cause brief stress-related paranoia/dissociation; sustained psychosis requires broader evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Borderline → **dialectical behavior therapy**; structured psychotherapy and consistent team boundaries
Trait-matched psychotherapy, e.g., avoidant → **CBT**, assertiveness training; clear expectations, empathic, nonpunitive tone
No medication treats personality disorder globally; target comorbid depression/anxiety or limited severe symptoms
Self-harm threats → assess intent, plan, access and safety; imminent risk → emergency psychiatric care
Avoid staff splitting through shared care plans; avoid reflexive long-term benzodiazepines in impulsive patients

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-injury/suicide, substance misuse, impaired work/relationships; antisocial traits → legal or violence consequences
Stigma and inconsistent treatment worsen engagement; therapeutic ruptures require careful repair

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: early developmental social-communication differences and restricted interests
Delusional disorder: fixed delusion rather than generalized suspicious personality style

personality-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Common diagnostic confusions
rows: Reactive hours-long shifts vs sustained mood episodes
Odd beliefs vs persistent frank psychosis

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

pituitary-adenomas.name: Pituitary adenomas
pituitary-adenomas.scope: Prolactinoma, acromegaly, nonfunctioning adenoma, pituitary apoplexy
pituitary-adenomas.core: Pituitary tumors cause hormone excess, pituitary failure, or sellar mass effects; determine functional status before choosing medical treatment or surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most sporadic; MEN1 with associated parathyroid/pancreatic endocrine tumors
Apoplexy may follow tumor hemorrhage/infarction, anticoagulation, pregnancy or major physiologic stress

rows.label: Clues
items: Mass effect → headache and bitemporal hemianopia from optic-chiasm compression
Pituitary failure → fatigue, hypotension, low libido; prolactin-related gonadal suppression may cause infertility
★ **Sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, hypotension** → pituitary apoplexy
GH excess may cause macroglossia, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet and worsening ring/shoe size

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autonomous secretion causes hormone excess; stalk compression interrupts dopamine inhibition, modestly raising prolactin
Expanding sellar tissue compresses normal pituitary and optic pathways; acute infarction can eliminate ACTH reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hormonal assessment → **contrast pituitary MRI**; formal visual fields if lesion abuts chiasm
Check prolactin, IGF-1, AM cortisol, free T4/TSH and gonadal axis; screen cortisol excess when clinically suspected
Elevated prolactin → exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and dopamine-blocking drugs
Large mass with unexpectedly modest prolactin → dilute assay for **hook effect**
Acromegaly: elevated age-adjusted IGF-1 → failure of GH suppression after oral glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected apoplexy → **IV hydrocortisone immediately**, fluids, urgent MRI and neurosurgical/endocrine assessment
Persistent severe visual deficits or reduced consciousness → urgent decompression after stabilization
★ Replace glucocorticoids **before levothyroxine** when both axes deficient
Prolactinoma → **cabergoline**, even with visual deficits; older exam questions may expect bromocriptine
Residual GH excess after surgery → octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant; radiation for selected refractory tumors

rows.label: Complications
items: Visual loss, adrenal crisis, hypogonadism; surgery → CSF leak, diabetes insipidus or panhypopituitarism
Acromegaly → cardiomyopathy, diabetes, sleep apnea, colon neoplasia; cabergoline → nausea/orthostasis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Craniopharyngioma: suprasellar cystic/calcified lesion, often childhood onset
Primary hypothyroidism: ↑TSH/↓free T4 with secondary prolactin elevation; medication effect: no autonomous tumor secretion

pituitary-adenomas.evidence: Prolactinoma checked 2026-10-30: [Pituitary Society consensus, 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-023-00886-5); other sellar emergencies: established teaching.

table.title: Subtype-directed management
rows: Observe if small; surgery for compression

pityriasis-rosea.name: Pityriasis rosea
pityriasis-rosea.scope: Herald patch, Christmas tree distribution, collarette of scale, viral prodrome, distinction from secondary syphilis, symptomatic management
pityriasis-rosea.core: Single herald patch followed days later by smaller oval scaly plaques in a Christmas tree pattern.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most common in adolescents and young adults

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Collarette of scale** just inside plaque edge; lesions follow cleavage lines on trunk
Possible viral prodrome; pruritus variable; palms, soles and mucosa usually spared

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Self-limited papulosquamous eruption; suspected viral reactivation, unproven cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis with typical evolution and distribution
Atypical rash, palmoplantar lesions, or sexual risk → syphilis serology
KOH scraping if annular plaque could represent dermatophyte infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reassurance: spontaneous resolution usually within 6–8 weeks
★ Pruritus → topical hydrocortisone or oral cetirizine; emollients
Severe widespread eruption → consider acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Temporary postinflammatory pigment changes, especially in darker skin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Secondary syphilis: palmoplantar lesions, generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches
Tinea corporis: advancing outer scale, central clearing, positive KOH
Guttate psoriasis: drop-like lesions after streptococcal pharyngitis, no preceding solitary plaque

pityriasis-rosea.evidence: Checked American Academy of Dermatology pityriasis rosea diagnosis and treatment guidance.

pneumothorax.name: Pneumothorax
pneumothorax.scope: Spontaneous pneumothorax (primary, secondary), tension pneumothorax, needle decompression, chest tube thoracostomy
pneumothorax.core: Pleural air causes acute unilateral pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds; circulatory compromise indicates tension physiology requiring immediate decompression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: tall thin young adults, smoking, family history
Secondary: COPD, cystic fibrosis, PJP, interstitial lung disease; trauma/procedures or positive-pressure ventilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral hyperresonance, dyspnea, asymmetric chest expansion; severity depends on underlying reserve
★ **Hypotension + distended neck veins + unilateral absent breath sounds** → tension; tracheal deviation is late
Ventilated: positive pressure converts occult pneumothorax to tension; sudden desaturation, rising airway pressure, collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of negative pleural pressure permits lung collapse
One-way air entry increases intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and causing obstructive shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable tension suspicion → **clinical diagnosis; no imaging delay**
Stable → upright chest radiograph: visceral pleural line with absent peripheral markings
Bedside ultrasound: absent sliding/B-lines supports; lung point highly specific; absent sliding alone nonspecific
CT for uncertain/complex cases; supine radiograph may show deep sulcus rather than apical air

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension → **immediate needle or finger thoracostomy**, then chest tube; oxygen and resuscitation
Needle commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space anterior/midaxillary, or second midclavicular; insert above rib
★ Minimal symptoms, stable: primary (any size) or small iatrogenic → **observation**, reliable follow-up
Symptomatic/large primary → aspiration or small-bore chest tube; secondary generally admit, drain if symptomatic/significant
Persistent air leak, recurrence, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation → VATS bleb treatment/pleurodesis

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, tension progression, recurrence; reexpansion pulmonary edema after drainage
Chest tube → bleeding, infection, organ injury; blocked/clamped drain may recreate tension

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**; avoid flying until radiographic resolution and clearance
Scuba diving contraindicated without specialist assessment/definitive prevention; counsel recurrence warning symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: pleuritic pain with preserved lung sliding, embolic risk
Giant bulla: intraparenchymal thin wall; CT if stable uncertainty before tube
Tamponade: shock with pericardial fluid rather than unilateral absent ventilation
Massive hemothorax: dullness, collapsed neck veins rather than distended

pneumothorax.evidence: Conservative care checked 2026-10-30: [BTS pleural guideline 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784); tension rescue: established emergency teaching.

polycystic-ovary-syndrome.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.scope: Rotterdam criteria (hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries), metabolic risks, weight loss, oral contraceptives, ovulation induction (letrozole, clomiphene)
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.core: Hyperandrogenism and chronic ovulatory dysfunction after exclusion of alternative causes suggest PCOS; management follows metabolic, menstrual and fertility priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, insulin resistance and obesity; lean patients can also have PCOS
Pubertal transition can mimic disease, requiring stricter adolescent diagnostic criteria

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular/infrequent menses, episodic heavy bleeding, infertility, hirsutism, acne or androgenic alopecia
Acanthosis nigricans suggests hyperinsulinemia; obesity is supportive, not required
Rapid virilization, deep voice or markedly elevated androgens → investigate tumor rather than assume PCOS

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin resistance and ovarian androgen excess impair follicular maturation and ovulation
Absent cyclic progesterone permits persistent estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adults: **2 of 3 Rotterdam** features—hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovarian morphology
Exclude mimics: **hCG, TSH, prolactin, morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone**; latter screens nonclassic CAH
Total/free testosterone; **clinical hirsutism/acne** suffices despite normal levels; DHEAS if adrenal source suspected
★ Irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism → **ultrasound not required**; LH:FSH ratio not diagnostic
BP, lipid profile and **oral glucose tolerance test** assess metabolic risk; adolescent diagnosis avoids ultrasound criteria

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Lifestyle/weight management first for all; modest weight loss can restore ovulation in overweight patients
★ No pregnancy desired → **combined OCP** for cycles/androgen symptoms; cyclic progestin or LNG-IUD protects endometrium
Persistent hirsutism → spironolactone with reliable contraception; allow months for hair response
Metabolic risk/insulin resistance → metformin; less effective than OCP for androgen symptoms
★ Anovulatory infertility → **letrozole first-line**; clomiphene alternative, older exams may expect it; check other factors

rows.label: Complications
items: Endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, infertility, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, OSA and depression
Pregnancy → increased gestational diabetes and hypertensive-disorder risk
Gonadotropin ovulation induction → high multiple-gestation risk, so letrozole/clomiphene first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for prolonged amenorrhea; persistent abnormal bleeding → endometrial assessment
Periodic glycemic/BP/lipid reassessment; preconception metabolic optimization and folate

rows.label: Mimics
items: Androgen-secreting tumor: rapid progression, severe virilization
Nonclassic CAH: elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: low estrogen with exercise/energy deficit

postpartum-care.name: Postpartum care
postpartum-care.scope: Normal puerperal changes, lochia, uterine involution, perineal and cesarean wound healing, breastfeeding, postpartum depression screening, routine postpartum visit
postpartum-care.core: Postpartum care is an ongoing assessment of recovery, mood, infant feeding, contraception, and chronic disease after every birth.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ All postpartum patients; assess support, sleep, safety, sexual health, and reproductive goals

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Contact within **3 weeks**; comprehensive visit by **12 weeks**, with earlier risk-based review
Hypertensive disorder → BP within 7–10 days; severe hypertension → within 72 hours

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Edinburgh or PHQ-9 depression screen; assess suicidality directly after positive self-harm response
BP, bleeding, fundal tenderness; inspect perineum/incision for erythema, drainage, separation
Observe latch/milk transfer; frequent feeds, lactation support; cracked nipples → correct positioning

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Heavy bleeding (pad soaked <1 hour), fever, dyspnea, severe headache → urgent evaluation
Mood screen positive → diagnostic interview, psychotherapy/SSRI; psychosis → emergency hospitalization
Increasing wound pain/purulence → evaluate infection; breast fluctuance → ultrasound for abscess

rows.label: Traps
items: Ovulation may precede first period; discuss contraception before discharge
Lactational contraception: amenorrhea, exclusive frequent breastfeeding, infant <6 months
Postpartum hypertension and cardiomyopathy can first appear after discharge

table.title: Expected recovery
rows: Red rubra → pink serosa → white/yellow alba
Descends daily; near prepregnancy size by 6 weeks
Pain improves; pulling normal if intact; keep clean
Early cramping and fluid loss; breastfeeding intensifies cramping

postpartum-care.evidence: Visit timing checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG postpartum care](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care); normal physiology established teaching.

postpartum-mood-disorders.name: Postpartum mood disorders
postpartum-mood-disorders.scope: Postpartum blues (onset <2 weeks, self-limited, reassurance), postpartum depression (MDD criteria, Edinburgh screening, SSRIs, psychotherapy), postpartum psychosis (delusions, infanticide risk, emergent hospitalization)
postpartum-mood-disorders.core: After birth, distinguish transient tearfulness from sustained depressive illness and from psychosis threatening maternal or infant safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior depression/postpartum depression, anxiety, poor support, trauma, sleep loss, pregnancy complications
★ **Bipolar disorder or previous postpartum psychosis** → especially high psychosis recurrence risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Anhedonia, guilt, impaired bonding/function, appetite/sleep changes beyond infant-care demands
★ **Suicidality, command hallucinations, infant-focused delusions**, confusion, mania → emergency
Unwanted distressing intrusive thoughts with preserved insight differ from fixed psychotic beliefs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormonal withdrawal, circadian disruption, and psychosocial stress interact with mood-disorder vulnerability
Postpartum psychosis frequently represents a bipolar-spectrum episode rather than schizophrenia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or PHQ-9** screens; positive result requires diagnostic interview
MDD: ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood/anhedonia, ≥2 weeks, clinically significant impairment
★ Screen for **bipolar disorder before antidepressants**; assess suicide/infant-harm intent, access, supervision
Check TSH/CBC for suggestive medical mimics; mania/psychosis → urgent psychiatric assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Ensure safe infant care, assess support, address sleep; do not leave psychotic patient alone with infant
Depression: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe → SSRI, often sertraline during breastfeeding
Severe postpartum depression: specialist-directed zuranolone or other treatment; weigh sedation and feeding considerations
Psychosis: inpatient antipsychotic ± lithium; ECT for severe, catatonic, suicidal, or refractory illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, infanticide, impaired attachment/child development, recurrent depressive or bipolar episodes

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protect sleep, mobilize family support; prior severe illness → antenatal psychiatric plan and postpartum prophylaxis
Repeat mood screening through pregnancy/postpartum; establish follow-up before discharge

rows.label: Mimics
items: Postpartum thyroiditis: biochemical thyroid dysfunction with systemic features
Normal adjustment: transient stress without pervasive anhedonia or sustained impairment

table.title: Course and disposition
rows: Persistent symptoms; may occur throughout first year
Outpatient treatment if safe; escalate for severity
Emergency hospitalization; protect mother and infant

postpartum-mood-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG screening](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/patient-screening), [2026 zuranolone update](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000006093); other management established teaching.

potassium-disorders.name: Potassium disorders
potassium-disorders.scope: Hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, cardiac membrane stabilization, shift therapy, elimination
potassium-disorders.core: Potassium abnormalities can cause weakness and fatal arrhythmias; stabilize cardiac risk while identifying the cause and correcting total-body balance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hyperkalemia: AKI/CKD, RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue lysis, insulin deficiency
Hypokalemia: GI losses, loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, insulin/beta-agonists, magnesium depletion

rows.label: Clues
items: Flaccid weakness, paralysis, palpitations; symptoms may be absent despite dangerous levels
★ **K ≥6.5 mmol/L, ECG changes, or rapid rise** → emergency; normal ECG not reassuring
Bradycardia/high-degree AV block with renal failure → suspect hyperkalemia; calcium before pacemaker

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extracellular K changes alter membrane excitability and cardiac conduction
Acidosis/insulin deficiency shift K outward; intracellular shifts can coexist with severe total-body depletion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG + repeat potassium**, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, magnesium; assess drugs and acid-base status
Hemolysis, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis → pseudohyperkalemia; repeat atraumatic draw if clinically compatible
Hypokalemia: urine K distinguishes renal wasting from extrarenal loss; interpret with BP/acid-base pattern
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory blood draw when malignant ECG changes present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hyperkalemic ECG changes or dialysis-patient arrest → **IV calcium gluconate/chloride first**; protects myocardium only
★ Shift K inward: **IV insulin + dextrose**, nebulized albuterol; bicarbonate mainly with significant acidosis
Remove K: loop diuretic if urine output, selected binders; urgent dialysis for severe refractory/renal-failure cases
Mild/stable hypokalemia → oral KCl; <2.5, arrhythmia, paralysis, or no oral access → monitored IV replacement
★ **Correct magnesium deficiency** for refractory low K; never give IV potassium push; monitor glucose after insulin

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, respiratory muscle failure
Overcorrection, rebound dyskalemia; insulin-induced hypoglycemia; IV potassium extravasation/phlebitis
Diuretic hypokalemia → **digoxin toxicity**, multifocal PVCs; check K first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review supplements/salt substitutes; monitor K/creatinine after diuretic or RAAS-drug changes
Treat diarrhea/vomiting and underlying mineralocorticoid disorders; replace ongoing losses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexic weakness without explanatory electrolyte pattern
Periodic paralysis: episodic shifts, sometimes thyrotoxicosis; avoid excessive replacement causing rebound

table.title: ECG patterns
rows: Peaked T → PR prolongation → wide QRS/sine-wave
Flat T, ST depression, prominent U waves

potassium-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established electrolyte emergency principles.

prelabor-rupture-of-membranes.name: Prelabor rupture of membranes
prelabor-rupture-of-membranes.scope: Term PROM (induction vs expectant), PPROM (<34 weeks), latency antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection, complications (chorioamnionitis, placental abruption, pulmonary hypoplasia)
prelabor-rupture-of-membranes.core: Membrane rupture before labor: term PROM favors induction; stable early PPROM favors monitored pregnancy prolongation with infection prevention and fetal maturation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previous PPROM/preterm birth, genital infection, smoking, short cervix, uterine overdistension

rows.label: Clues
items: Sudden gush or persistent watery leakage; reduced fluid volume may develop
★ Fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia → **intra-amniotic infection**; pain/bleeding → possible abruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Membrane weakening permits fluid loss and ascending infection; latency inversely related to gestational age

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sterile speculum examination**: pooling or fluid leaking from cervical os
Nitrazine alkaline pH and ferning support diagnosis; blood, semen, vaginitis cause false-positive pH
Equivocal → amniotic protein assay; ultrasound supports, never independently confirms rupture
★ Avoid **digital cervical examinations** unless delivery imminent; assess fetal status and presentation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Infection, fetal compromise, significant abruption, or prolapsed cord → **deliver regardless of gestational age**
Expectant <34 weeks → 7-day latency antibiotics: IV ampicillin/erythromycin then oral amoxicillin/erythromycin
Azithromycin may replace erythromycin; avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate because neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis risk
Preterm birth expected → complete **betamethasone ×2, 24 hours apart**; magnesium sulfate if birth <32 weeks
GBS-positive/unknown-risk labor → penicillin; avoid late-preterm latency antibiotics and prolonged tocolysis

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal/neonatal infection, prematurity, placental abruption, cord compression/prolapse
Early prolonged rupture → pulmonary hypoplasia and limb contractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: Stop smoking, treat identified infections, manage short cervix/prior preterm birth risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Urinary leakage: urine odor, no pooling/ferning
Physiologic leukorrhea: nonwatery discharge without amniotic-fluid markers

table.title: Stable PROM without delivery indication
rows: Oxytocin induction; brief expectant option after counseling
Delivery or expectant management; stop expectance by 37
Individualized counseling: termination versus expectance, maternal risks

pressure-injuries.name: Pressure injuries
pressure-injuries.scope: Stage 1 through 4 pressure injuries, unstageable eschar, risk assessment (Braden scale), pressure offloading, repositioning, wound debridement, dressing selection
pressure-injuries.core: Sustained pressure and shear damage skin and deeper tissue over bony prominences or beneath medical devices.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Immobility, spinal cord injury, impaired sensation, poor perfusion, malnutrition
Moisture/incontinence, friction, advanced age; oxygen tubing and immobilization devices create focal loading

rows.label: Clues
items: Sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, occiput and device contact sites; pain may precede visible injury
Dark skin: assess temperature, induration and discoloration rather than redness alone
Purulence, spreading erythema, fever or worsening pain → infection; exposed bone raises osteomyelitis concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary compression and tissue deformation → ischemia/reperfusion damage; shear increases deep injury
Surface appearance may underestimate muscle injury; stages describe depth, not a required progression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspect skin and document depth**, drainage, undermining and surrounding tissue
Braden scale assesses sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition and friction/shear
Suspected osteomyelitis → MRI and, when feasible, bone biopsy/culture; superficial swabs poorly specific
Healing lesions retain their original highest stage; **never reverse-stage**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Offload pressure**, support surfaces and individualized repositioning; float heels with pillows under calves
Saline cleansing; shallow/low-exudate → hydrocolloid; draining → foam/alginate; maintain moisture, protect surrounding skin
★ Necrotic tissue → debridement, except **stable dry heel/ischemic eschar** without infection
Systemic antibiotics only for cellulitis, sepsis or osteomyelitis; not colonization alone
Deep defects → **oral protein/calorie supplements** if malnourished, not parenteral; then negative-pressure, flap closure

rows.label: Complications
items: Cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis, chronic pain and functional decline

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily skin checks, mobilization, moisture barriers and adequate protein/calories
Avoid donut cushions, massage over prominences; reassess device fit and risk whenever clinical status changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incontinence dermatitis: diffuse superficial moisture-associated damage, not focal loading
Arterial ulcer: distal ischemic site, weak pulses

table.title: Stage by visible depth
rows: Partial thickness; exposed dermis or serum blister
Full thickness; fat visible; no deep structures
Exposed/palpable fascia, muscle, tendon or bone
Persistent maroon/purple discoloration or blood blister

preterm-labor.name: Preterm labor
preterm-labor.scope: Preterm labor (<37 weeks), cervical insufficiency, tocolysis (indomethacin, nifedipine), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, GBS chemoprophylaxis
preterm-labor.core: Regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; briefly delay eligible early births to improve neonatal outcomes, without prolonging unsafe pregnancies.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior spontaneous preterm birth, short cervix, multiple gestation, infection, smoking, uterine anomalies
Cervical surgery or prior painless second-trimester loss suggests cervical insufficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Pelvic pressure, backache, increased discharge, contractions; assess membrane rupture and bleeding
Fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia → intraamniotic infection; maternal/fetal instability changes delivery timing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature inflammatory/uterine activation versus mechanically weak cervix with painless dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sterile speculum examination** for pooling and cervix; ultrasound dates pregnancy and assesses presentation
Transvaginal cervical length; selected symptomatic cases: negative fetal fibronectin predicts low imminent birth risk
Collect GBS culture, urine studies; exclude previa before digital examination with bleeding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Birth within 7 days, **24–33 6/7 weeks** → betamethasone; selected untreated 34–36 6/7-week pregnancies also eligible
★ Delivery expected <32 weeks → **magnesium sulfate** for neuroprotection, not primary tocolysis
Tocolysis: 48 hours for steroids/transfer; no maintenance; late-preterm steroids avoided with pregestational diabetes
★ **No tocolysis** with infection, significant abruption, severe preeclampsia, or fetal compromise; proceed toward delivery
Intrapartum penicillin for positive/unknown GBS; no routine antibiotics for intact membranes without infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, sepsis, cerebral palsy; magnesium toxicity → hyporeflexia, respiratory depression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Singleton short cervix ≤20 mm before 24 weeks → vaginal progesterone; consider at 21–25 mm
Cervical insufficiency/prior qualifying loss → cerclage; prior preterm birth + cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks
17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate withdrawn 2023; progesterone without short cervix not routinely recommended
Older exam questions may expect 17-hydroxyprogesterone from 16–20 weeks after prior spontaneous preterm birth

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: no progressive dilation
Cervical insufficiency: painless dilation, minimal contractions
PPROM: membrane rupture precedes labor; distinct latency-antibiotic pathway

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists
DiGeorge: 3rd/4th **pharyngeal pouch** failure → absent thymus, hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, T-cell infections
ADA deficiency: autosomal recessive SCID; toxic deoxyadenosine destroys T and B cells

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vertical HIV: bacterial infections + zoster, nodes, maternal opportunistic infection; low CD4, positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

primary-immunodeficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical immunology teaching.

professional-boundaries.name: Professional boundaries
professional-boundaries.scope: Romantic relationships with current patients, romantic relationships with former patients, gift acceptance, maintaining professional objectivity, chaperone use
professional-boundaries.core: Preserve professional judgment and protect patients from exploitation arising from the physician's position of trust.

rows.label: Principle
items: Power imbalance and confidential knowledge can persist after care ends

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Offer a trained **chaperone** for intimate exams; honor requests; document presence or refusal
Explain examination, obtain consent, provide draping, and stop if consent withdrawn
Discuss boundary concerns respectfully; arrange safe transfer if objectivity is impaired

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **No romantic or sexual relationship with a current patient**, regardless of apparent consent
Decline costly gifts, cash, or gifts linked to preferential care or influence

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Former patient: assess residual dependence, vulnerability, prior treatment and exploitation risk
Modest culturally customary gift acceptable if judgment and equitable care unaffected

rows.label: Traps
items: Ending care to pursue romance does not erase power imbalance; psychotherapy warrants heightened caution
Chaperone presence does not substitute for the patient's consent

professional-boundaries.evidence: Checked AMA Code of Medical Ethics opinions on romantic relationships, gifts and chaperones.

pubertal-development.name: Pubertal development
pubertal-development.scope: Tanner stages, normal thelarche vs breast mass, premature adrenarche, precocious puberty, constitutional delay of growth and puberty
pubertal-development.core: Interpret sexual maturation by sequence, age, growth velocity, and bone age; isolated benign variants lack progressive gonadal activation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constitutional delay often familial; chronic illness, undernutrition, excess exercise delay maturation
CNS lesions, gonadal/adrenal hormone excess, exogenous sex steroids can cause early puberty

rows.label: Clues
items: Girls: breast budding precedes peak growth, then menarche about 2–3 years later
Boys: testes enlarge before penile growth; pubic hair reflects adrenarche, not necessarily gonadarche
★ Asymmetric tender **subareolar breast bud** at expected age usually normal; hard eccentric mass needs evaluation
Rapid height acceleration, advancing secondary characteristics, neurologic symptoms → pathologic early maturation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central puberty: hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility → LH/FSH → gonadal steroids
Adrenarche produces adrenal androgens independently; peripheral hormone excess suppresses pituitary gonadotropins
Immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis → irregular anovulatory cycles, normal for 2–3 years after menarche
Virilized boy with **prepubertal testes** → peripheral androgen, usually adrenal; central puberty enlarges testes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Precocious: secondary sexual development **before 8 years girls or 9 years boys**
★ Delayed: **no breasts by 13**, no testes ≥4 mL by 14; evaluate absent menarche by 15
Growth chart, Tanner examination, bone age; LH/FSH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH selected by pattern
Central precocity → pubertal basal/stimulated LH; brain MRI especially boys, young girls, neurologic signs
Peripheral pattern → targeted adrenal/gonadal tests/imaging; isolated adrenarche requires exclusion of rapid virilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Progressive central precocity → **GnRH agonist**; treat CNS cause when present
Peripheral precocity → remove hormone source or treat tumor/adrenal disorder; GnRH agonist alone ineffective
Constitutional delay → reassurance, follow growth; distress → specialist-guided brief sex-steroid course
Benign premature thelarche/adrenarche → observe progression; no automatic hormonal treatment
Pubertal gynecomastia, unilateral or bilateral, smooth subareolar → **reassurance**; no labs/biopsy; carcinoma very rare

rows.label: Complications
items: Early epiphyseal closure → reduced adult height; psychosocial distress
Missed hypogonadism → impaired bone accrual; untreated CNS/tumor cause may progress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, manage chronic disease, avoid household hormone exposure; serial growth surveillance
Normal puberty + moodiness, mild parent conflict → **puberty education** for child, parents; no drug testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary gonadal failure: high LH/FSH, low sex steroids
Permanent central hypogonadism: absent progression rather than eventual familial catch-up
Familial short stature: short parents, bone age matches chronologic age; constitutional delay: **delayed bone age**

table.title: Tanner staging anchors
rows: Further enlargement; menarche usually within 1–2 years

pubertal-development.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric endocrine timing and Tanner staging.

raynaud-phenomenon.name: Raynaud phenomenon
raynaud-phenomenon.core: Episodic cold- or stress-triggered digital vasospasm produces reversible color changes; asymmetric painful attacks or tissue injury suggest secondary disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young women, family history; smoking, vibration tools, cold exposure
Systemic sclerosis, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease; stimulants, beta blockers, ergot derivatives

rows.label: Clues
items: Pallor → cyanosis → reactive redness; numbness or tingling; all three phases not required
★ Digital **ulcers, pitting scars, gangrene** require evaluation for secondary vasculopathy
Sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, reflux, inflammatory arthritis, rash, or dyspnea → connective tissue disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Exaggerated arteriolar smooth-muscle constriction; secondary disease adds endothelial injury and structural vasculopathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical history + nailfold capillaroscopy**; inspect pulses and both hands
Suspected secondary disease → ANA, ESR/CRP, CBC, urinalysis; disease-specific antibodies based on findings
Suspected proximal/occlusive disease → arterial Doppler and vascular consultation
Normal inflammatory tests do not override tissue-threatening clinical findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warm core and hands, stop nicotine and vasoconstricting drugs; **dihydropyridine CCB** for persistent symptoms
Nifedipine or amlodipine first-line; monitor headache, edema, hypotension
CCB-refractory or CCB-intolerant → sildenafil or topical nitrate; do not combine PDE-5 inhibitor with nitrates
★ Critical ischemia → urgent admission, **IV prostacyclin**, vascular/rheumatology consultation; treat underlying disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary disease → infection, ulceration, infarction, tissue loss
Primary disease rarely causes permanent damage; evolving systemic findings warrant reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Layered clothing, gloves, avoid rapid temperature changes; stress management and vibration-exposure reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acrocyanosis: persistent painless blue hands, no discrete attacks
Erythromelalgia: burning red extremities worsened by heat
Peripheral arterial disease: persistent ischemia with diminished pulses

raynaud-phenomenon.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatology teaching.

research-ethics.name: Research ethics
research-ethics.scope: Institutional review board (IRB), vulnerable populations (prisoners, children), coercion and undue inducement, clinical equipoise, informed consent in research
research-ethics.core: Scientifically valid research requires independent oversight, fair selection, favorable risk-benefit balance, and voluntary informed participation with additional safeguards for vulnerability.

rows.label: Principle
items: Respect for persons, beneficence, justice: autonomy, minimize harm, equitable recruitment
★ **Clinical equipoise**: expert uncertainty about superior treatment; personal doubt insufficient
Vulnerability warrants safeguards, not automatic exclusion from scientifically justified studies

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **IRB approval before recruitment**; disclose conflicts, monitor harms, report unexpected problems
Explain purpose, randomization, risks, uncertain benefits, alternatives, privacy, injury care, contacts
★ **Ongoing consent**: check understanding, answer questions, update risks; withdrawal without penalty

rows.label: Don't
items: Coercion: threaten lost care, employment, grades, liberty for refusal; parole offer to prisoners
Undue influence: incentives distort voluntary judgment; reasonable reimbursement/payment permitted
Placebo causing serious harm by withholding proven care; disguise research as personalized treatment

rows.label: Exceptions
items: IRB waiver: minimal risk, impracticable otherwise, preserved rights/welfare; later disclosure when needed
Identifiable-data waiver: study also impracticable without identifiers
Emergency research: prior regulatory safeguards/approval; treatment emergency exception insufficient

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **IRB approval never replaces informed consent** unless an authorized waiver applies
Capable child's dissent generally respected despite parental permission
Therapeutic misconception: participant assumes every study decision maximizes personal clinical benefit

table.title: Additional safeguards
rows: Parental permission plus developmentally capable child's assent
Permitted research category; prisoner representative on IRB
Legally authorized representative; seek participant assent

rh-alloimmunization.name: Rh alloimmunization
rh-alloimmunization.scope: Rh(D) and other red cell alloimmunization (Kell, Duffy), anti-D immune globulin prophylaxis, indirect Coombs titer monitoring, fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke), middle cerebral artery Doppler for fetal anemia
rh-alloimmunization.core: Maternal IgG against fetal red-cell antigens crosses the placenta, causing fetal anemia, hydrops, and neonatal hemolysis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antigen-negative mother/positive fetus; prior pregnancy, transfusion, bleeding, trauma, invasive procedures
Anti-D, anti-Kell, and anti-Duffy clinically significant; ABO incompatibility usually milder

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic mother; fetal ascites, skin edema, placentomegaly, cardiomegaly
Neonate: early jaundice, pallor, reticulocytosis, **positive direct Coombs**; severe disease → cardiovascular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: First exposure sensitizes; subsequent antigen exposure produces an anamnestic response
Kell antibodies additionally suppress erythropoiesis; low titers can still cause severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First prenatal visit: ABO/Rh type + **indirect Coombs**; repeat before routine antenatal prophylaxis
Antibody → **paternal antigen typing**; negative (certain paternity) → no fetal risk; else fetal typing, titers
★ Critical titer, often **1:16**, or previously affected pregnancy → middle cerebral artery Doppler
MCA peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM → fetal blood sampling; Kell warrants specialist surveillance
Kleihauer-Betke quantifies hemorrhage for dosing: **300 µg covers 30 mL fetal whole blood**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe preterm fetal anemia → **intrauterine transfusion**; near term → delivery
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → phototherapy; severe hemolysis → exchange transfusion

rows.label: Complications
items: High-output heart failure, stillbirth, bilirubin encephalopathy, delayed neonatal anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Unsensitized Rh-negative mother: **anti-D immune globulin** at 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum
Sensitizing event → dose now; lasts ~12 weeks, repeat at 28; postpartum only if Rh-positive/unknown infant
★ Established anti-D sensitization → prophylaxis ineffective; no equivalent prophylaxis for Kell/Duffy
ACOG 2024: routine Rh testing/prophylaxis may be forgone for abortion/loss before 12 weeks

rows.label: Mimics
items: Parvovirus: nonimmune hydrops with negative maternal antibody screen
ABO hemolysis: may affect first pregnancy; fetal hydrops uncommon

rh-alloimmunization.evidence: Prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG Rh guidance](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/the-rh-factor-how-it-can-affect-your-pregnancy), [2024 update](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000005733); remaining content established teaching.

rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid-arthritis.scope: Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, anti-CCP and RF, DMARDs (methotrexate, biologics), extra-articular manifestations, Felty syndrome, cervical spine subluxation
rheumatoid-arthritis.core: Persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness and improvement with activity; early disease-modifying treatment prevents erosions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Female sex, smoking, family history, HLA-DRB1 susceptibility; onset often middle adulthood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boggy swelling of **MCP, PIP, wrists**; DIP joints usually spared
Ulnar deviation, swan-neck/boutonnière deformities; subcutaneous nodules and constitutional symptoms
Extra-articular: pleuritis, interstitial lung disease, episcleritis/scleritis, pericarditis, neuropathy
★ **Felty syndrome**: established erosive disease + splenomegaly + neutropenia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoimmune synovial inflammation → pannus, cartilage destruction, marginal bone erosion
TNF and other inflammatory cytokines drive articular and systemic injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical synovitis → **anti-CCP, RF, ESR/CRP**; anti-CCP more specific, negative serology not exclusionary
Hand/foot radiographs: periarticular osteopenia, uniform narrowing, erosions; early films can be normal
Acute single hot joint → arthrocentesis to exclude infection or crystals before attributing symptoms
Neck pain, neurologic symptoms, or suspected instability before anesthesia → cervical imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Methotrexate + folate** first-line for moderate/high activity; hydroxychloroquine reasonable for low activity
Treat to remission/low activity; inadequate response → add biologic, often TNF inhibitor
NSAIDs relieve symptoms without preventing joint damage; glucocorticoid bridge only briefly when necessary
Methotrexate: avoid pregnancy, significant liver disease; monitor CBC, creatinine, LFTs
TNF inhibitors: avoid active infection, advanced heart failure, demyelinating disease

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Atlantoaxial subluxation** → cord compression; protect cervical spine during airway management
Accelerated cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, secondary amyloidosis; immunosuppression → serious infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, occupational/physical rehabilitation; assess bone and cardiovascular risk
Screen TB and hepatitis B before biologics; update vaccines before immunosuppression

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteoarthritis: bony DIP/first CMC enlargement, brief stiffness
Psoriatic arthritis: dactylitis, nail pitting, asymmetric or DIP involvement
SLE arthritis: usually nonerosive, rash/cytopenias, disease-specific autoantibodies

routine-prenatal-care.name: Routine prenatal care and early pregnancy
routine-prenatal-care.scope: Pregnancy diagnosis (beta-hCG), initial prenatal assessment, routine first-trimester screening, aneuploidy screening
routine-prenatal-care.core: Confirm and date pregnancy, assess maternal risks, offer one aneuploidy-screening strategy or diagnostic testing, and arrange time-sensitive prenatal studies.

rows.label: Who
items: All pregnancies; review obstetric history, drugs, illness, substance use, violence, family history
Offer carrier screening and genetic counseling; discuss patient preferences and right to decline

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Early visit: urine hCG confirms pregnancy; serum quantitative hCG for uncertain/complicated cases
★ First-trimester **ultrasound crown–rump length** best establishes gestational age
Serum screen 10–13 6/7 weeks; NT 11–13 6/7; cfDNA from 10 weeks

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Initial **CBC, ABO/Rh, antibody screen, urine culture**; HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, HCV, rubella immunity
GC/chlamydia by age/risk; offer one aneuploidy strategy regardless of maternal age
Anatomy ultrasound 18–22 weeks; AFP for open neural tube defects when not otherwise assessed

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Abnormal screen → counseling, ultrasound, **CVS/amniocentesis** before irreversible decisions
CVS: 10–13 weeks; amniocentesis: ≥15 weeks; neither automatically required after negative screening
